subject: Last year ignored in yearlySiteCovs for pcountOpen

messages.author: e394633264e35c35
messages.subject: Last year ignored in yearlySiteCovs for pcountOpen
parts:
In the help page for pcountOpen, it says the last year is ignored from yearlySiteCovs for omega & gamma.  I am using dynamics='trend' with yearlySiteCovs for omega and I'm confused about how to setup the yearlySiteCovs data frame.  Are the covariates (x) of omega taken from year t or t-1?  In other words,

N[i,t] = N[i,t-1] * omega( x[i,t] )

or

N[i,t] = N[i,t-1] * omega( x[i,t-1] )

If the last year of yearlySiteCovs is ignored, it has the be the second one, correct?  

Thanks,
Doug Leasure

messages.author: 20119867e986c754
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Last year ignored in yearlySiteCovs for pcountOpen
parts:
Richard can jump in here and correct me if I'm wrong, but I think I know the answer to this one:
 
First off, when you use dynamics="trend" in pcountOpen you omit the omega parameter and the trend (actually the finite rate of population increase) is represented by gamma.
 
Then, yes, the last value of the yearly site covs is ignored for the analysis, just like in the default parameterization. You can convince yourself of this by putting NA for the last value and you will see you get the same result.
 
Finally, I think your two equations for N[i,t] are both slightly off.  It might be better represented by this:
 
N[i,t] ~ Poisson(lambda)
N[i,t+1] ~ Poisson(N[i,t] gamma)
 
It gets complicated when thinking about how to model it or present the results because the finite rate of increase (gamma) which is our estimate of trend is calculated for the interval between two sampling periods. Thus, when you have yearly site covs, there will be one less value for gamma than for the N's.

messages.author: 20119867e986c754
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Last year ignored in yearlySiteCovs for pcountOpen
parts:
In my way of thinking, the gamma covariates aren't taken from year t or year t-1. The covariates for a gamma parameter in year t are taken from the interval from year t-1 to year t. If you have 10 years of survey data you will have 10 estimates of abundance, but only 9 estimates of the finite rate of increase (usually called lambda, but called gamma here since lambda is used already). Thus, for each covariate on gamma (i.e yearly site covariate) you will need 9 columns of actual data and a 10th column that is not used. There is a one-to-one correspondence between the gamma values and the gamma covariates.
 
If you have a covariate for the "trend" in the population that is only measured each year at the same time you do your survey, then you will have to decide whether you think the value from t-1 or from t will best explain the trend in the population. In the anlaysis I am working on we have a value that is measured during the interval between surveys that we think should affect the trend in the population.
